title: Four-word latent-state proxies do not reliably protect a boundary test
statement: In a synthetic pilot, stratifying fixed-cell complete-word shuffles by an independent four-word proxy for each line’s latent state fails to control latent-line confounding. Out of 30 generated books per setting, the binary proxy rejects all 30 at each state accuracy 0.7, 0.8 and 0.9; a five-level count proxy rejects 28, 30 and 22 respectively. At accuracy 1 it rejects none, but the target groups are immovable, so that case has no power. The independent-word condition rejects once in 30 with either proxy. These results concern a synthetic equality statistic, not a held-out manuscript fact.
check: Do not register this proxy-conditioned null as a direct-transition test. Develop controls with calibrated latent-state uncertainty, movement and support criteria, and assess false rejection over a wider preregistered family of latent models. Test calibrated positive alternatives, missing data, varying page effects, vocabulary and line lengths, exact marginal preservation, dependent endpoints and sparse groups; implement a reviewed primitive only after controls demonstrate adequate size and power. Then fix the intended eight edge pairs and aggregate statistic before comparing both manuscript witnesses on held-out pages.
design: Each seeded book has six pages, 36 lines per page and 12 two-bit words per line. A line independently receives a binary latent state. In latent settings, each word’s first and last bit is independently the latent state with probability p, otherwise its complement; conditional on the state there is no direct predecessor-to-successor influence. The independent condition draws both bits independently with probability 0.5. In the positive Markov setting, last bits retain p=0.8 latent dependence, while each target word from index 5 onward copies the previous word’s last bit as its first bit with probability 0.85, otherwise flips it.
test: The four initial words are excluded from the tested boundaries and used as a proxy: either whether at least two of their last bits are one, or the exact count 0–4. Test seven boundaries between positions 4–11 with the one-sided number where previous last bit equals next first bit. Shuffle complete words jointly within page, exact target position, and proxy class; the baseline omits proxy class. Hence adjacent boundaries share the same permuted word and the probe does not overlap test positions. For each book and method use 99 shuffles, seeded 10000+book seed, and p=(1+#shuffles with statistic >= observed)/100; repeat book seeds 0–29. This statistic is a simple surrogate, not the parent proposal’s eight-pair aggregate.
limits: The probe is noisy and conditioning on a noisy latent surrogate leaves residual mixture dependence. At p=1 all target words are identical within each page-position-proxy group, so the proxy permutation is immovable and its lack of rejection does not show valid calibrated inference; an implementation with a movement gate must refuse the test. This study has only 30 books and 99 permutations per setting, binary glyphs and one line-state process; the same seed indices are shared across settings. Positive-control rejection rates do not establish general power. No manuscript data were examined, no hidden-page test performed, and this is not a trusted scorer primitive.
